9701-13.1.1.motivate: You can recognise a hydrocarbon by checking its elements, regardless of its shape or size.
9701-13.1.1.establish: A hydrocarbon is a compound made up of carbon and hydrogen atoms only. A formula containing oxygen, nitrogen or a halogen is not a hydrocarbon, even if most atoms are carbon and hydrogen.
9701-13.1.1.connect: This definition identifies alkanes and alkenes as hydrocarbons, but excludes alcohols and carboxylic acids.
9701-13.1.1.note:
- Hydrocarbon: carbon and hydrogen atoms only.
- Any other element excludes the compound.
9701-13.1.1.self_explain: Why is ethanol not a hydrocarbon even though it contains carbon and hydrogen?

9701-13.1.2.motivate: A molecule can be organic without possessing a characteristic functional group.
9701-13.1.2.establish: Alkanes are simple, saturated hydrocarbons. They contain carbon and hydrogen only and have carbon–carbon single bonds. Alkanes have no functional group; their C–C and C–H bonds form the hydrocarbon framework rather than a distinctive group such as C=C or –OH.
9701-13.1.2.connect: Compare an alkane with an alkene: the alkene has a C=C functional group, which gives it characteristic addition reactions.
9701-13.1.2.note:
- Alkanes are simple hydrocarbons.
- Alkanes have no functional group.
- Saturated means carbon–carbon single bonds only.
9701-13.1.2.self_explain: Why does the presence of C–H bonds not make an alkane a functional-group compound?

9701-13.1.3.motivate: Two compounds with similar carbon skeletons can react differently because one group changes.
9701-13.1.3.establish: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic chemical reactions. In the syllabus classes, the group dictates chemical properties and strongly influences physical properties. For example, an alkene contains C=C, an alcohol –OH, an aldehyde –CHO, a ketone an internal C=O, a carboxylic acid –COOH, and an ester –COO–. Halogenoalkanes, acyl chlorides, amines, amides and nitriles have their own identifying groups. Members of one homologous series share the same functional group and characteristic reactions.
9701-13.1.3.connect: First identify the group, then use the formulas and naming rules for that class.
9701-13.1.3.note:
- Functional groups give characteristic reactions.
- They influence physical and chemical properties.
- One homologous series shares one functional group.
9701-13.1.3.self_explain: Why do propene and propanol have different characteristic reactions?

9701-13.1.4.motivate: One molecule can be represented in four ways; each representation answers a different question.
9701-13.1.4.establish: A general formula expresses the composition of a homologous series using $n$, such as $\ce{C_nH_{2n+2}}$ for acyclic alkanes. A structural formula shows atom and group connectivity in condensed form. A displayed formula shows every atom and every bond, including O–H. A skeletal formula shows the carbon framework as lines: each unlabelled end or vertex is carbon, and carbon-bound hydrogens are omitted. Infer them by giving each carbon four bonds. Show heteroatoms and hydrogens on them. Interpret and use these representations for the syllabus classes, including hydrocarbons, halogenoalkanes, alcohols, carbonyl compounds, acids, esters, acyl chlorides, amines, amides and nitriles.
9701-13.1.4.connect: Count skeletal atoms and complete valencies before deducing a molecular formula.
9701-13.1.4.note:
- General formula: series composition using $n$.
- Structural formula: condensed connectivity.
- Displayed formula: all atoms and bonds.
- Skeletal formula: carbon at each unlabelled end and vertex.
9701-13.1.4.self_explain: What must you add mentally when reading a skeletal formula?

9701-13.1.5.motivate: A systematic name lets someone reconstruct a molecule's connectivity.
9701-13.1.5.establish: For simple aliphatic molecules up to six carbons, choose the longest parent chain containing the principal functional group. Number it to give that group the lowest locant. Use a carbon stem from meth- through hex-, indicate substituents and their positions, and give the class suffix, for example propan-2-ol or butanoic acid. Include a nitrile carbon in the parent count. For straight-chain esters $\ce{RCOOR'}$, name the O-bonded alkyl $\ce{R'}$ first and the acid-derived alkanoate part second; up to six carbons may occur in each ester part. This syllabus restricts esters and nitriles to straight chains.
9701-13.1.5.connect: The functional group identified first determines the suffix and often controls numbering.
9701-13.1.5.note:
- Choose the parent chain containing the main group.
- Number for the lowest functional-group locant.
- Ester: O-bonded alkyl name, then alkanoate.
- Count nitrile carbon in its parent chain.
9701-13.1.5.self_explain: Which part of methyl propanoate supplies the word methyl?

9701-13.1.6.motivate: A drawing tells you the actual atom count; a simplest ratio may hide that count.
9701-13.1.6.establish: Deduce a molecular formula by counting all atoms in a structural or displayed formula. In a skeletal formula, count every unlabelled end and vertex as carbon, then supply carbon-bound hydrogens to complete carbon valency four, accounting for double or triple bonds. Include shown heteroatoms and their hydrogens. The molecular formula records actual numbers of atoms. The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio: divide all molecular subscripts by their greatest common factor. For $\ce{C4H8O2}$ this gives $\ce{C2H4O}$.
9701-13.1.6.connect: A correct skeletal count is the input for both formulas; only the empirical formula is reduced.
9701-13.1.6.note:
- Molecular formula: actual atom counts.
- Complete skeletal carbon valencies before counting H.
- Empirical formula: simplest whole-number ratio.
9701-13.1.6.self_explain: Why is $\ce{C2H4O}$ empirical but not molecular for methyl ethanoate?
